KNN is called a lazy learning algorithm because it doesn’t build a model during training; it simply stores the training data and makes predictions at runtime.

Introduction

1.1 Background and Motivation
Supply chains are held together by contracts. Every relationship between a buyer and a supplier, between a manufacturer and a logistics provider, between a procurement team and a vendor is governed by a legally binding agreement that specifies what must be delivered, when, at what price, and what happens when something goes wrong.

price, and what happens when something goes wrong. These contracts carry risk in every clause: a payment term that is ambiguous, a liability cap that is too low, a force majeure clause that does not cover pandemic disruption, or a delivery obligation that can be misread. Identifying these risks before signing is the fundamental purpose of contract review.

The problem is scale. A single procurement team at a mid-sized company might manage hundreds of active supplier contracts at any time.

hundreds of active supplier contracts at any time. Reading each one carefully enough to identify every risk-relevant clause is time-consuming, expensive, and imperfect. Industry research consistently shows that contract errors — clauses that were present but misunderstood, or risks that were present but missed — are among the most common sources of commercial disputes.

ng the most common sources of commercial disputes. The manual nature of the process is both the root cause of the problem and the bottleneck that prevents organisations from scaling their contract risk management as their supplier networks grow.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) has matured considerably in the last decade.

(NLP) has matured considerably in the last decade. The advent of transformer-based language models — BERT in 2018, domain-adapted variants like Legal-BERT shortly after — has demonstrated that machines can now read and classify legal text with meaningful accuracy. Researchers have applied these tools to construction contracts, terms of service agreements, and SEC filings.

cts, terms of service agreements, and SEC filings. What has not been done, as this research will show, is applying them specifically to supply chain contracts: the agreements that govern procurement, delivery, liability, and vendor relationships in operational supply chains.

This thesis addresses that gap.

This thesis addresses that gap. Using the Contract Understanding Atticus Dataset (CUAD) — a professionally annotated benchmark of 510 real commercial contracts — it builds and evaluates a four-stage NLP pipeline for automatically detecting and classifying risk clauses in supply chain contracts. The pipeline progresses from a simple TF-IDF baseline through to Legal-BERT, a transformer model pre-trained on 12GB of legal text.

ansformer model pre-trained on 12GB of legal text. The results are concrete, reproducible, and commercially significant: Legal-BERT identifies every force majeure clause in the test set without a single miss and achieves a macro F1-score of 0.966 across six risk clause categories.

1.2 Problem Statement
The central problem this research addresses can be stated precisely: procurement and legal teams spend substantial time and resources reviewing supply chain contracts to identify risk-relevant

g supply chain contracts to identify risk-relevant clauses, yet this process is manual, slow, and error-prone. Current practice relies almost entirely on human readers — lawyers, paralegals, and procurement professionals — to scan contract text and flag clauses that carry financial, operational, or legal risk. This approach has three compounding weaknesses.

First, it does not scale.

compounding weaknesses.

First, it does not scale. As supplier networks grow, the volume of contracts requiring review grows with them, but the capacity of human review teams does not grow proportionally. Organisations either review fewer contracts thoroughly or more contracts superficially — both outcomes increase risk.

Second, it is inconsistent. Different reviewers applying the same criteria to the same contract may flag different clauses, or miss the same clauses in different ways.

auses, or miss the same clauses in different ways. There is no guarantee of uniform coverage across a contract portfolio.

Third, it is expensive. Based on conservative estimates of junior legal analyst compensation (approximately €24 per hour) and review throughput (approximately 25 pages per hour), reviewing 100 contracts of 80 pages each for six risk categories costs approximately €92,000 per year in labour alone.

ts approximately €92,000 per year in labour alone. This does not account for the cost of errors — risk clauses that were present but not flagged.

NLP-based automation offers a potential solution to all three problems simultaneously: it scales linearly with the volume of contracts, applies the same classification criteria consistently across every clause it processes, and can reduce review costs by an estimated 80–90% for the categories it handles reliably.

ted 80–90% for the categories it handles reliably. The research question is therefore not whether automation is desirable in principle, but whether NLP models can achieve the classification accuracy required for deployment in a real procurement context.

2.2 NLP in Legal and Contract Text Analysis
